paras: The lynching of Aaron Bean took place near Jasper, Texas, on Wednesday, October 3, 1888, when a mob took Bean, a Black man, from officers on the road to jail and shot him to death. Bean had been accused of accosting the young daughter of a Magnolia Springs farmer while she was riding and dragging her from her saddle. The killing was known outside Texas through a single Galveston wire dispatch, which several papers printed under headlines approving of it.

According to the dispatch, the young daughter of John Lee, "a prominent farmer of Magnolia Springs," was out horseback riding when she was accosted by Bean, who was also on a horse. She whipped her horse into a run to escape, but, the report said, he overtook her and dragged her from her saddle. The girl's name, age and race are not given, and the account of the encounter comes from the unnamed source of the wire report, with nothing from Bean's side.

At that point a party of white men came upon the scene, wounded Bean, arrested him and turned him over to the sheriff. On the road to the jail a mob formed, took him from the officers, and "riddled [him] with bullets." The dispatch called the killers "a mob of infuriated citizens" but named none of them, gave no number, and did not name the sheriff or the officers escorting Bean.
The Galveston version gave the day only as Wednesday. A copy of the same account datelined Jasper, October 4, placed the killing "near here yesterday," and a weekly news summary dated it "on the 3d."
No report of an inquest, of an arrest of any member of the mob, or of grand jury action appears in the coverage.

The dispatch, datelined Galveston, October 5, appeared that day in the Washington Evening Star and the Alexandria Gazette. On October 6 it ran in the Richmond Dispatch, the Memphis Appeal, the Savannah Morning News, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and the Indianapolis Journal. Weeklies carried it through mid-October, among them the Weekly Courier-Journal of Louisville, the Emporia Weekly News, the Newberry Herald and News, and, as late as October 19, the Phillipsburg Herald in Kansas. News-in-brief columns cut it to a line or two, the Wheeling Register calling Bean "a Texas negro who attempted rape" and the Hickman Courier and Ohio Democrat saying he "attempted to outrage" the girl.

Because the body text was nearly identical from paper to paper, headlines carried most of the editorial judgment. The Memphis Appeal ran the dispatch under "The Good Old Texas Way," and the Weekly Courier-Journal under "Very Properly Lynched." The Savannah Morning News headed its copy "An Attempt to Outrage a Girl Avenged by Citizens." Other headlines labeled Bean "A Negro Fiend" in the Alexandria Gazette, "A Brute" in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and "A Negro Brute" in the Phillipsburg Herald.

The Newberry Herald and News presented the lynching as a rescue, under "A Lady's Narrow Escape" and a subhead saying she was "Rescued by a Party who Lynch the Negro." The Jasper-datelined copy wrote "The black fiend" into the body of the story itself. A few papers, including the Richmond Dispatch and the Indianapolis Journal, used plain headings such as "Negro Killed by a Mob." Every version treated the accusation as established fact, and none carried any account from Bean or anyone speaking for him.

accounts.label: Galveston wire report
accounts.gist: Word 'has been received' that Bean accosted and dragged Lee's daughter from her horse, was wounded and arrested by white men, and was taken from officers on the road to jail and riddled with bullets by a mob of infuriated citizens.

accounts.label: Jasper-datelined version
accounts.gist: The same account datelined Jasper, Oct. 4, placing the killing 'near here yesterday' and calling Bean 'The black fiend.'

accounts.label: News summaries
accounts.gist: One- or two-line items saying Bean attempted to 'outrage', 'rape' or 'assault' the girl and was killed by a mob, one dating it 'on the 3d.'

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headed the dispatch 'The Good Old Texas Way.'
The Weekly Courier-Journal headed it 'Very Properly Lynched.'
The Savannah Morning News called the killing 'An Attempt to Outrage a Girl Avenged by Citizens.'
Headlines labeled Bean 'A Negro Fiend', 'A Brute' and 'A Negro Brute', and the Newberry Herald and News framed the lynching as a rescue ('A Lady's Narrow Escape').
The Richmond Dispatch, Evening Star and Indianapolis Journal printed the wire under descriptive headlines ('A Negro Shot by an Infuritated Mob', 'Negro Killed by a Mob').

conflicts.note: All versions place the killing on Wednesday, October 3 (also 'on the 3d', A15); the Evening Star's Oct. 6 dateline in an Oct. 5 paper is a misprint. Not a substantive dispute.

versions.value: Accosted, pursued and dragged her from her saddle
'attempted to outrage' / 'attempted rape' / 'an attempt to assault'

conflicts.note: The full dispatch describes only an encounter on horseback ending with the girl dragged from her saddle; condensed items and headlines restated it as attempted rape. None of these is an independent source.

record_check.dossier: The name is Aaron Bean (OCR 'Bcan'); no paper states the race of John Lee or his daughter.

record_check.record: said to have accosted and dragged a young white woman from her horse
record_check.dossier: Said to have accosted and dragged 'the young daughter of John Lee' from her horse; her race is not stated.
The only injury reported is Bean's own wound before arrest; he was then killed, so the count should be 0 separate injured.

The 'pursuit' in the papers is Bean's alleged pursuit of the girl; the white party 'came along' and wounded and arrested him. Acts against Bean: wounding/arrest, seizure from officers, shooting, killing.

record_check.record: accused of attempting to assault a girl
record_check.dossier: Supported, in the summaries' wording; the full dispatch says he accosted her and dragged her from her saddle.
